title: AWS API key hardcoded in mobile app bundle
summary: A live AWS access key was shipped inside the mobile app, where anyone can extract it. That single key could unlock cloud storage and services — and attackers scan for exactly this.
description: A hardcoded AWS access key/secret was found in the shipped mobile bundle and the git history. The key had broad S3 and SES permissions.
impact: Anyone who downloads the app can extract the key and access cloud resources — data theft, resource abuse (crypto-mining), or email spoofing via SES.
stepsToReproduce: Unzip and grep the JS bundle for AKIA
Recover a valid AWS access key + secret

evidence.title: Hardcoded credentials

remediation.recommendation: Revoke and rotate the key immediately. Never ship secrets to clients — proxy through the backend with short-lived, scoped credentials. Add gitleaks to CI and pre-commit. Scrub git history.
remediation.verification: Key revoked within the hour; CloudTrail showed no unauthorized use. gitleaks now runs in CI and blocks commits.

title: Weak password hashing (unsalted SHA-1)
summary: Passwords are protected with an old, fast, unsalted hashing method (SHA-1). If the database ever leaks, attackers could crack most passwords quickly using standard tools.
description: Password hashing uses unsalted SHA-1. This is fast to brute-force and vulnerable to rainbow tables, so a database breach would expose most user passwords.
impact: In a breach, weak hashing turns a data leak into mass account compromise and credential-stuffing against other services.

evidence.title: Insecure hashing

remediation.recommendation: Migrate to a slow, salted password hash (Argon2id or bcrypt). Re-hash on next login, and force resets for stale accounts.

title: Vulnerable dependency (lodash) with known CVE
summary: A third-party library used by the API was several versions out of date and had a publicly known security bug with a ready-made exploit. Updating it closes the hole.
description: `lodash@4.17.11` is affected by CVE-2021-23337 (command injection via template). A public exploit exists.
impact: Depending on usage, an attacker could achieve command injection through the vulnerable code path. Even where not directly exploitable, it signals stale dependency hygiene.

remediation.recommendation: Upgrade lodash to a patched version; enable Dependabot/renovate and fail CI on high-severity advisories; maintain an SBOM.

title: Staff susceptible to credential-harvesting phishing
summary: In a simulated phishing test, 6 of 40 staff entered their password into a fake login page. Phishing-resistant MFA stopped account takeover, but the human risk remains and needs ongoing training.
description: A red-team phishing campaign captured credentials from 15% of targeted staff. FIDO2/passkey MFA prevented actual account takeover, but weaker second factors would not have.
impact: Phishing remains the most likely path to initial access. Without phishing-resistant MFA everywhere, captured credentials would enable account takeover and lateral movement.

evidence.title: Phishing landing page (lab)
evidence.description: The lookalike login page used in the authorised campaign.

remediation.recommendation: Roll out phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys/FIDO2) org-wide, enforce DMARC/DKIM/SPF, add an easy report-phish button, and run quarterly training. Risk formally accepted for residual human factor with these controls in place.

timeline.note: Passkey rollout started; residual risk accepted with compensating controls

title: Over-permissive CI/CD token in GitHub Actions
summary: The build pipeline runs with far more permissions than it needs and pulls unpinned third-party actions. A poisoned dependency or action could ride the pipeline straight into production.
description: The deploy workflow grants `permissions: write-all` and references third-party actions by mutable tags. A compromised action or dependency could exfiltrate secrets or tamper with releases.
impact: Supply-chain compromise: a single poisoned dependency or action could reach production and every environment that runs the release.

evidence.title: Excessive permissions & unpinned action
evidence.content:
permissions: write-all            # BUG: far too broad
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: some-org/deploy-action@main  # BUG: mutable tag, not pinned

remediation.recommendation: Apply least-privilege `permissions:` per job, pin actions to commit SHAs, use OIDC instead of long-lived secrets, and run builds on isolated runners with an SBOM.

title: Server-Side Request Forgery in webhook validator
summary: A feature that checks a user-supplied webhook URL can be tricked into calling internal systems — including the cloud metadata service — potentially leaking internal credentials.
description: The webhook validation endpoint fetches an arbitrary user-supplied URL server-side with no allow-list, enabling SSRF to internal addresses including 169.254.169.254.
impact: Access to internal-only services and potentially cloud instance credentials via the metadata endpoint, enabling further compromise.
stepsToReproduce: Observe the server fetch and return internal metadata

remediation.recommendation: Allow-list destination hosts/schemes, resolve and block private/link-local ranges, disable redirects, and use IMDSv2. Fetch from an egress-restricted network.
